92580.m: Light-coloured clothes are easier to see at night.

92581.q: Why do colourful curtains at a sunny window fade over time?
92581.e: Above all the invisible UV light of the sun breaks down dyes little by little. That is why the colours become pale.

92582.q: What do glow-in-the-dark stars on the bedroom ceiling do when you switch off the light?
a: They keep glowing for a while
92582.e: Glow-in-the-dark paint stores some of the light. In the dark it slowly gives it off again as a faint, often greenish glow.
92582.m: Glow-in-the-dark paint keeps glowing for a while in the dark.

92583.q: Which colour comes right next to red in the rainbow?
92583.e: The colours in the rainbow are always in the same order. Orange comes straight after red.
92583.m: In the rainbow, orange follows red.

92584.q: At what time of day are you most likely to see a rainbow?
92584.e: A rainbow only appears when the sun is low. If the sun is too high, the bow lies below the horizon.
92584.m: Rainbows are usually seen in the morning or evening.

92585.q: What happens if you try to walk to the end of a rainbow?
a: It gets bigger and stays still
92585.e: A rainbow is not a thing in a fixed place. It depends on where you are standing and moves with you.
92585.m: You can never reach a rainbow.

92586.q: What shape would a rainbow have if the ground weren't in the way?
92586.e: From the ground you only see part of the circle. From an aeroplane you can sometimes see the whole circle.
92586.m: A rainbow is really a circle.

92587.q: Can you see a rainbow at night too?
92587.e: With a bright full moon and rain, a moonbow can appear. It is faint and usually looks whitish.
92587.m: Rarely there is a moonbow too.

92588.q: What material is a prism for light experiments usually made of?
92588.e: A prism has to be transparent so that light can pass through it. That is why it is usually made of glass or clear plastic.
92588.m: A prism is made of transparent glass.

92589.q: Which colour is bent the least by a prism?
92589.e: Each colour is bent by a different amount in the glass. Red is bent the least.
92589.m: Red light is bent the least in a prism.

92590.q: What happens if you bring the coloured light from a prism back together?
92590.e: With a lens or a second prism you can combine the colours again. Then white light appears again.
92590.m: All the colours together make white light again.

92591.q: What happens to red laser light in a prism?
a: It stays red and is only bent
92591.e: Red laser light has only one colour. The prism can bend it, but it can't split it into more colours.
92591.m: Light of one colour stays one colour in a prism.

92592.q: What happens to the direction of a beam of light in a prism?
a: It turns round in a circle
92592.e: Light is bent when it goes into the glass and out again at an angle. This bending is called refraction.

92593.q: What at a window can throw colourful spots of light onto the wall?
92593.e: A cut crystal has many slanted faces. It works like a prism and splits the sunlight.
92593.m: Glass crystals at the window make colourful spots of light.

92594.q: Which gemstone sparkles in many colours because it splits light like a prism?
92594.e: A cut diamond bends light very strongly. That is why colourful flashes appear in it.
92594.m: Diamonds sparkle in colours because they split light.

92595.q: Apart from a prism, what can split sunlight into colours?
92595.e: Water bends light in a similar way to glass. If a full glass of water stands in the sun, you sometimes see colourful stripes.
92595.m: Water can also split light into colours.

92596.q: Which three colours are often called the primary colours in art lessons?
92596.e: You can mix many other colours from these three paints. This grouping is often taught in art lessons.
92596.m: Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours in the paint box.

92597.q: From which three colours of light does a screen make all its colours?
92597.e: A screen has tiny dots of light in three colours. Depending on how brightly they shine, we see different colours.
92597.m: Screens mix all colours from red, green and blue.

92598.q: Apart from black, which colour cartridges does a colour printer have?
92598.e: Printers mix colours from cyan (blue-green), magenta (pinkish red) and yellow. Black is added for dark areas.
92598.m: A colour printer prints with cyan, magenta and yellow.

92599.q: Can you mix a primary colour from other colours?
92599.e: Primary colours are the starting colours. You need them to mix other colours, not the other way round.

92600.q: Which of these colours is not a primary colour in the paint box?
92600.e: In the paint box, green is not one of the three primary colours. You can make it yourself.
92600.m: Green is not a primary colour in the paint box.

92601.q: What are colours that you mix from two primary colours called?
92601.e: Orange, green and violet are each made from two primary colours. That is why they are called secondary colours.
92601.m: Two primary colours make a secondary colour.

92602.q: What is the smallest number of primary colours you need to mix very many colours with paint?
92602.e: With three suitable primary colours you can mix almost all bright colours. With only two, many shades are missing.
92602.m: Three primary colours are enough for very many mixed colours.

92603.q: Which colour do you get if you mix yellow and blue paint?
92603.e: When painting, yellow and blue make green. With more yellow, the green gets lighter.

92604.q: Which colour do you get from red and yellow paint?
92604.e: Red and yellow together make orange. That is the colour of an orange or a carrot.

92605.q: Which colour do you get from red and blue paint?
92605.e: If you mix red and blue, you get violet. With more blue it gets darker.

92606.q: Which colour do you get if you mix red with lots of white?
92606.e: White makes a colour lighter. So red becomes a light pink.

92607.q: What do you get if you mix black and white paint?
92607.e: Black and white make grey. The more black, the darker it gets.

92608.q: What do you usually get if you mix lots of paints together?
92608.e: Each paint swallows part of the light. If you mix many, almost everything is swallowed and the colour becomes dark.
92608.m: Lots of paints together become dark.

92609.q: Which colour do you get when red and green light fall on the same spot?
92609.e: Light mixes differently from paint. To our eyes, red and green light together look yellow.
92609.m: Red and green light make yellow.

92610.q: Which colour do you get when red and blue light shine together?
92610.e: Red and blue light make a strong pink. This colour is called magenta.
92610.m: Red and blue light make magenta.

92611.q: Which colour can't you mix with paints?
92611.e: When you mix paints, they always swallow more light. That is why you can't mix white; you need it as a colour of its own.
92611.m: You can't mix white from paints.

92612.q: What is the invisible light that comes after violet called?
92612.e: Ultraviolet means “beyond violet”. Our eyes can't see this light, but it can cause sunburn.

92613.q: What is the invisible light beyond red that we feel as warmth called?
92613.e: Infrared means “below red”. We feel it, for example, as the warmth of a stove.

92614.q: What colour is a white sheet of paper when only red light falls on it?
92614.e: White paper reflects any light that falls on it. If only red light reaches it, it looks red.
92614.m: White paper shows the colour of the light.

92615.q: Which light looks more yellowish than white?
92615.e: A candle flame gives off more red and yellow light than blue. That is why its light looks warm and yellowish.

92616.q: What does a white T-shirt often look like under black light?
92616.e: Many washing powders contain brighteners. These turn the lamp's invisible light into visible bluish light.
92616.m: Under black light, white clothes glow bluish.

92617.q: What colour is the Sun when you see it from space?
92617.e: In space there is no air to scatter parts of the light. That is why the Sun looks white there.
92617.m: From space the Sun looks white.

92618.q: What do you get when a red, a green and a blue lamp shine on the same spot?
92618.e: To our eyes, the three colours of light together make white.
92618.m: Red, green and blue light together make white.

92619.q: What is the band of all colours that white light can be split into called?
92619.e: The spectrum goes from red to violet. A rainbow shows it in the sky.
92619.m: White light can be split into a spectrum.

92620.e: On the colour wheel, the colours go round in order. That way you can see which colours are related.
92620.m: On the colour wheel, the colours go round in a circle.

92621.q: Which colour is opposite red on the colour wheel?
92621.e: Opposite colours are very different. The opposite colour of red is green.
92621.m: Red and green are opposite each other on the colour wheel.

92622.q: Which colour is opposite blue on the colour wheel?
92622.e: Blue and orange make a strong pair of colours. Next to each other they look especially bright.
92622.m: Blue and orange are opposite each other on the colour wheel.

92623.q: What are colours that are opposite each other on the colour wheel called?
92623.e: Complementary means “completing”. These colours complete each other and make a strong contrast.
92623.m: Opposite colours are called complementary colours.

92624.q: Which Swiss artist drew a famous colour wheel with twelve colours?
92624.e: This painter and teacher from Bern worked at the Bauhaus. His twelve-part colour wheel is still used in schools today.
92624.m: Johannes Itten designed a famous colour wheel.

92625.q: Which famous German poet studied a colour wheel?
92625.e: The poet wrote a thick book about colours, the “Theory of Colours”. In it he also drew a colour wheel.
92625.m: Goethe wrote a Theory of Colours.

92626.q: Which colours are called warm colours?
92626.e: These colours remind us of fire and the sun. That is why they look warm.
92626.m: Red, orange and yellow are warm colours.

92627.q: What sometimes shimmers in bright colours on a puddle in the road?
92627.e: A wafer-thin layer of oil floats on the water. Light is reflected from its top and bottom and creates colours.
92627.m: A thin film of oil shimmers in rainbow colours.

92628.q: Which bird has large, shimmering tail feathers with eye patterns?
92628.e: The male peacock spreads out a fan of splendid feathers. Depending on the angle, they shimmer green, blue and gold.

92629.q: Why does the underside of a CD shine in bright colours?
a: It gives off its own light
92629.e: On a CD, tiny grooves run close together. They bend the light and split it into colours.
92629.m: Fine grooves make a CD shimmer in colours.

92630.q: What shimmers on the inside of some seashells?
92630.e: Mother-of-pearl is made of many wafer-thin layers. They make the light shimmer in colours.

92631.q: Where does the brilliant blue of some butterfly wings come from?
a: From tiny structures on the scales
92631.e: On the wing scales there are tiny ridges. They mainly reflect blue light, without any blue pigment.
92631.m: Some blue comes from tiny structures, not from pigment.

92632.q: What happens to shimmering colours when you change the angle you look from?
92632.e: Shimmering colours depend on how the light reaches your eyes. If you turn your head, they change.
92632.m: Shimmering colours change with the angle you look from.

92633.q: Which beetle often shimmers metallic green?
92633.e: The shell of the rose chafer shines green like metal. Depending on the light, it also shimmers gold or copper.

92634.q: Which colourful bird by Swiss streams has shimmering blue feathers?
92634.e: The kingfisher's blue comes from fine structures in its feathers. That is why it shines differently depending on the light.
92634.m: The kingfisher has shimmering blue feathers.

92635.q: Why does the sky often glow red in the evening?
a: The light has a long way to travel through the air
The sun gets hotter in the evening
92635.e: When the sun is low, its light has to pass through a lot of air. The blue light is scattered away, and red and orange are left.
92635.m: In the evening the sky is red because the light has a long way to travel.

92636.q: What colour is the sun often when it sets?
92636.e: Just above the horizon, much of the blue part of sunlight is missing. That is why the sun looks orange-red.
92636.m: The setting sun is often orange-red.

92637.q: What is the red glow of mountain peaks at sunset called?
92637.e: The high peaks are still lit by the reddish light of the sun while the valley is already dark. You often see this in Switzerland.
92637.m: Mountains glowing red is called alpenglow.

92638.q: What often makes a red evening sky especially strong?
a: Lots of snow on the ground
92638.e: Tiny dust particles scatter the light even more. After volcanic eruptions or with Saharan dust, the evening sky is often especially colourful.
92638.m: Dust in the air makes the red evening sky stronger.

92639.q: In which direction do you see the red evening sky?
92639.e: The sun sets in the west. That is where the sky glows red in the evening.
92639.m: You see the red evening sky in the west.

92640.q: Why isn't the sun red at midday?
a: Its light has a short way through the air
The clouds are gone at midday
The moon is in front of it
92640.e: At midday the sun is high and its light only passes through a little air. So almost all the colours are kept.
92640.m: At midday, sunlight only travels a short way through the air.

92641.q: What colour is a sunset on Mars?
92641.e: The fine dust on Mars scatters light differently from our air. Photos from Mars rovers show bluish sunsets.

92642.q: What colour is the sky on the Moon?
92642.e: The Moon has no layer of air to scatter light. That is why the sky there is black, even during the day.
92642.m: On the Moon, the sky is black.

92643.q: How does the blue of the sky change high up in the mountains?
92643.e: High up there is less air above us. So less light is scattered and the sky looks dark blue.
92643.m: In the mountains, the sky is a darker blue.

92644.q: Why doesn't the air in a glass look blue?
a: There is far too little air
It is too warm in the glass
92644.e: The blue of the sky only comes from many kilometres of air. A glass full of air is not enough.
92644.m: Only a huge amount of air looks blue.

a: The water droplets scatter all colours equally
They are made of cotton wool
92645.e: The droplets in clouds are much bigger than the particles of air. They scatter all colours about equally, and that makes white.
92645.m: Clouds are white because they scatter all colours.

92646.q: Why do thunderclouds look dark grey?
a: They are so thick that little light gets through
92646.e: Thunderclouds are often many kilometres high. The light is scattered so many times inside them that little reaches the bottom.
92646.m: Thick clouds let little light through.

92647.q: Why does deep water in the sea or a lake look blue?
92647.e: Water swallows red light a little more strongly than blue light. So in deep water, mainly blue is left.
92647.m: Deep water looks blue because it swallows red.

92648.q: Why do faraway mountains often look bluish?
a: Because of all the air in between
Because they are made of blue stone
Because it is always night there
92648.e: There is a lot of air between us and the mountains. It scatters blue light into our eyes and gives the view a bluish tint.
92648.m: Distant mountains look bluish because of the air.

92649.q: What colour is the sky on Mars during the day?
92649.e: Fine reddish dust floats in the thin air of Mars. It colours the daytime sky yellowish to reddish brown.
92649.m: The daytime sky on Mars is reddish brown.

92650.q: What is visibility often like in Switzerland when the Föhn wind blows?
a: Very clear, you can see far
92650.e: The Föhn is a dry, warm wind that blows down from the mountains. The dry air is very clear, the mountains look close and the sky is deep blue.
92650.m: When the Föhn blows, you can often see very far.

92651.q: What does a red colour filter do with white light?
a: It only lets red light through
It only lets blue light through
92651.e: A filter swallows some of the colours. A red filter lets almost only red through.
92651.m: A red filter only lets red through.

92652.q: What does a red colour filter do with the other colours?
92652.e: The other colours are swallowed in the filter. Only red gets through.
92652.m: A colour filter swallows the other colours.

92653.q: Why does red writing on white paper disappear behind red film?
a: The writing and the paper look the same red
The film wipes the writing away
92653.e: Through the red film, only red light comes from the white paper. The red writing looks exactly the same and no longer stands out.
92653.m: Behind red film, red writing disappears.

92654.q: What does a green leaf look like through a red filter?
92654.e: The leaf mainly reflects green light. The red filter doesn't let green through, so the leaf looks dark.
92654.m: Green things look dark through a red filter.

92655.q: What happens if you hold a red and a green filter one behind the other?
92655.e: The first filter only lets red through. The second doesn't let red through, so hardly any light is left.
92655.m: Two different colour filters one behind the other let almost no light through.

92656.q: What do colourful church windows do with sunlight?
92656.e: The coloured glass works like a filter. That is why colourful patches of light fall on the floor inside the church.

92657.q: How did old traffic lights with a white bulb get their red light?
a: Through a red glass in front
Through red paint on the road
92657.e: In front of the bright lamp there was a coloured glass. It only let the red light through.
92657.m: Old traffic lights coloured their light with coloured glass.

92658.q: What does a yellow banana look like through blue film?
92658.e: The blue film lets almost only blue light through. But the banana hardly reflects any blue, so it looks dark.
92658.m: Through blue film, yellow things look dark.

92659.q: What does the world look like through glasses with yellow lenses?
92659.e: The yellow lenses swallow part of the blue light. That is why everything looks tinted yellow.
92659.m: Through yellow lenses, everything looks yellowish.

92660.q: What colours are the lenses of simple cardboard 3D glasses often?
92660.e: One lens is red, the other blue or blue-green. That way each eye only sees part of the picture.
92660.m: Simple 3D glasses have one red and one blue lens.

92661.q: Why do you see a picture in 3D with red and cyan 3D glasses?
a: Each eye sees a slightly different picture
92661.e: Two slightly shifted views are printed in the picture in two colours. Each lens only lets one view through, and the brain puts them together into a 3D picture.
92661.m: Two different pictures for the two eyes make a 3D picture.

92662.q: What do you often notice when you take off red glasses after a long time?
a: Everything looks greenish for a moment
Everything looks red for a moment
92662.e: The eye gets used to the red light and becomes less sensitive to red. After you take them off, the world briefly looks like the opposite colour.
92662.m: After red glasses, the world looks greenish for a moment.

92663.q: Why do skiers often wear goggles with yellow or orange lenses in fog?
a: You can see bumps in the snow better
92663.e: Yellow and orange lenses block a lot of scattered blue light. That makes bumps in the snow clearer.
92663.m: Yellow ski goggles help in fog.

92664.q: What does a blue sky look like through glasses with red lenses?
92664.e: Red lenses let hardly any blue light through. That is why the blue sky looks dark.
92664.m: Through red lenses, blue things look dark.

92665.q: Can special colour-filter glasses help people with red-green colour blindness?
a: Yes, some colours become easier to tell apart
Yes, they cure the eyes for ever
No, they are just for fun
92665.e: Glasses like these filter out certain parts of the light. This makes red and green stand out from each other better, but the colour blindness is not cured.
92665.m: Special glasses help some people tell colours apart better.

92666.q: Why do the colours of a film look strange through red and cyan 3D glasses?
a: Each eye only gets some of the colours
92666.e: The red lens only lets red through, the other only blue-green. The brain has to put together the colours from both eyes, and it doesn't do this perfectly.

92767.q: How does the ground move when an S-wave passes through?
a: Across the direction the wave travels
Only back and forth in the direction it travels
Not at all, it only travels through air
Only in circles at the surface
92767.e: S-waves are shear waves. The particles vibrate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels, a bit like a rope being shaken.
92767.m: With S-waves, the ground moves across the direction of travel.

92768.q: Which earthquake waves usually cause the most damage to buildings?
92768.e: Surface waves travel along the Earth's surface and have large movements. They arrive last, but they shake buildings the most.
92768.m: Surface waves cause most of the damage in earthquakes.

92769.q: How do some surface waves move the ground during an earthquake?
a: They make it roll up and down like waves in the sea
They lift it by a metre for ever
92769.e: With some surface waves, the particles of ground move in an ellipse. The ground rises and falls like the sea.
92769.m: Some earthquake waves make the ground roll up and down.

92770.q: How do Love waves shake the ground during an earthquake?
a: In a circle around the Earth's core
92770.e: Love waves are surface waves. They move the ground horizontally back and forth, across the direction of travel.
92770.m: Love waves shake the ground sideways back and forth.

92771.q: A P-wave travels through the Earth's crust at 6 km/s. How long does it take to travel 120 km?
92771.e: Time equals distance divided by speed. 120 km ÷ 6 km/s = 20 s.
92771.m: The travel time of a wave is the distance divided by the speed.

92772.q: Why do you sometimes hear a dull rumble during an earthquake?
a: Some of the ground waves pass into the air as sound
The Earth cracks open with a bang
The quake makes the wind stronger
The measuring instruments make the noise
92772.e: If the ground vibrates fast enough, it passes the movement on to the air. The first waves in particular can then be heard as a rumble or thunder.
92772.m: Earthquake waves can be heard as a rumble.

92773.q: How can earthquake waves be used to study the structure of the Earth's interior?
a: How they bend and how fast they travel reveal the layers of rock
They are used to drill holes down to the Earth's core
They bring rock samples to the surface
They colour the layers in the ground
92773.e: Earthquake waves are bent and reflected at the boundaries between layers and change speed depending on the material. From their arrival times at many stations, scientists build a picture of the Earth's interior.
92773.m: Earthquake waves look inside the Earth like X-rays look inside the body.

92774.q: What is the huge water wave called that a strong quake under the seabed can trigger?
92774.e: If the seabed suddenly rises or sinks, the whole column of water above it is moved. The wave can travel thousands of kilometres.
92774.m: An undersea earthquake can trigger a tsunami.

92775.q: Why do you often feel a jolt first and only then stronger shaking during a nearby quake?
a: The faster waves arrive before the slower ones
A quake always consists of two earthquakes
The ground has to warm up first
The air slows down the first waves
92775.e: Different earthquake waves travel at different speeds. The further away the source is, the bigger the time gap between them.
92775.m: Earthquake waves arrive one after another depending on their speed.

92776.q: What does the magnitude of an earthquake describe?
a: The strength of the quake at its source
The damage at a particular place
The length of the quake in minutes
92776.e: The magnitude is a measure of the energy released. It is calculated from measurements by seismometers.
92776.m: The magnitude measures the strength of an earthquake at its source.

92777.q: How is the intensity of an earthquake different from its magnitude?
a: It describes the effects at a particular place
It measures the depth of the source
It gives the time of the quake
It is always exactly twice as big
92777.e: A quake has only one magnitude, but a different intensity at every place. The intensity depends on what people feel and what gets damaged.
92777.m: The intensity describes how strongly a quake is felt at a place.

92778.q: Which instrument is used to measure earthquake waves?
92778.e: A seismometer records the tiniest movements of the ground. The location and magnitude of a quake are calculated from the measurements.

92779.q: Which scale for the strength of earthquakes is often mentioned in the news?
92779.e: The Richter scale was developed by Charles Richter in 1935. Today experts use similar scales, but the news often still talks about the Richter scale.
92779.m: The strength of earthquakes is often given on the Richter scale.

92780.q: Can the magnitude of an earthquake be negative?
a: Only for quakes under the sea
92780.e: The magnitude scale has no lower limit. Sensitive seismometers also measure tiny quakes with values below zero.
92780.m: Very small earthquakes can have a negative magnitude.

92781.q: With each step of magnitude, the energy increases about 32 times. How many times more energy does a magnitude 6 quake release than a magnitude 4 quake?
92781.e: Two steps mean 32 × 32 = 1024. That is about 1000 times more energy.
92781.m: Two steps of magnitude mean about a thousand times more energy.

92782.q: From what magnitude does an earthquake usually cause major damage in populated areas?
92782.e: You can hardly feel quakes below 3. From a magnitude of about 6, buildings often collapse, especially if they are not built to withstand earthquakes.
92782.m: Earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above are usually destructive.

92783.q: Who developed the best-known scale for measuring the strength of earthquakes in 1935?
92783.e: The American seismologist Charles Francis Richter presented his scale in 1935. It still bears his name today.
92783.m: Charles Francis Richter developed the Richter scale in 1935.

92785.q: What does an earthquake of magnitude 2 on the Richter scale mean for people?
a: You hardly feel it or not at all
92785.e: Quakes of magnitude 2 are very weak. They are recorded by instruments but usually not noticed by people.
92785.m: You can hardly feel earthquakes with a small magnitude.

92786.q: Roughly what magnitude does an earthquake have that can cause major damage?
92786.e: Quakes from magnitude 6 to 7 can badly damage houses. You can hardly feel quakes of around magnitude 1 or 2.
92786.m: Strong earthquakes have a magnitude of about 7.

92787.q: One quake has a Richter magnitude of 5, another of 2. How many times bigger is the swing on the seismogram for the stronger one?
92787.e: Each step means a swing ten times bigger, and the difference is three steps. 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.
92787.m: Three steps on the Richter scale mean a swing a thousand times bigger.

92788.q: Does the Richter scale have a fixed maximum value?
a: No, it has no upper limit
92788.e: The scale has no upper limit. But in nature, quakes far above magnitude 9.5 are hardly possible, because ruptures in rock cannot get endlessly big.
92788.m: The Richter scale has no upper limit.

92789.q: How much bigger is the swing on the seismogram at magnitude 6 than at magnitude 5?
92789.e: The Richter scale is built so that each step means a swing ten times bigger. So from 5 to 6 it is ten times as much.
92789.m: One step more on the Richter scale means a swing ten times bigger.

92790.e: A seismometer measures the movements of the ground. The strength of a quake is calculated from its recordings.

92791.q: On what principle does a classic seismometer work?
a: A heavy mass stays still while the ground moves
A thermometer measures the heat of the quake
A microphone listens to the rumbling in the ground
92791.e: The heavy mass hangs loosely in the casing. Because of its inertia it stays almost still, and the movement of the casing relative to the mass is measured.
92791.m: A seismometer uses the inertia of a mass.

92792.q: To which planet did the InSight probe take a seismometer in 2018 that ETH Zurich had helped to build?
92792.e: The InSight probe landed on Mars in November 2018. Its seismometer recorded more than 1300 marsquakes.
92792.m: There are quakes on Mars too.

92793.q: What did the seismometers set up on the Moon by Apollo astronauts detect?
a: A magnetic field like the Earth's
92793.e: The instruments recorded vibrations from 1969 to 1977. These included moonquakes and meteorite impacts.
92793.m: There are moonquakes on the Moon.

92794.q: Why are seismometers often placed in tunnels, caves or boreholes?
a: There, traffic and wind disturb the measurements less
They are closer to the Earth's core there
92794.e: Seismometers are very sensitive and also register lorries or gusts of wind. Underground they are better shielded from such disturbances.
92794.m: Underground, seismometers measure with less disturbance.

92795.q: What is the minimum number of measuring stations needed to find the epicentre of a quake from the distances?
92795.e: Each station only knows its distance to the quake, so a circle around itself. Only three circles cross at a single point.
92795.m: With three stations you can locate an epicentre.

92796.q: In which three directions does a modern seismometer measure ground movement?
a: Forwards, backwards and in a circle
To the north, to the Earth's core and to the sun
92796.e: Ground movement is three-dimensional. That is why a modern seismometer measures in three directions, one vertical and two horizontal.
92796.m: Modern seismometers measure in three directions.

92797.q: What is the curve recorded by a seismometer during an earthquake called?
92797.e: The seismometer records the ground movement as a zigzag line. This recording is called a seismogram. The stronger the quake, the bigger the swings.
92797.m: A seismogram shows the ground movement during a quake.

92798.q: What does a modern seismometer turn ground movement into?
92798.e: In the past, needles scratched the curves on paper. Today coils and sensors produce electrical signals that are stored and sent digitally.
92798.m: Modern seismometers deliver their measurements as electrical signals.

92799.q: What is the hypocentre of an earthquake?
a: The place inside the Earth where the rupture begins
The point with the most damage
The measuring station that notices the quake first
The highest point of the quake zone
92799.e: At the hypocentre, the rock begins to break. From there, earthquake waves spread out in all directions.
92799.m: The hypocentre is the source of an earthquake inside the Earth.

92800.q: Which term means the same as hypocentre?
92800.e: Hypocentre and focus are two names for the same place. “Hypo” is Greek and means “under”.
92800.m: Focus is another word for hypocentre.

92801.q: A source is 30 km deep, and a station is 40 km from the epicentre. How far is the station from the hypocentre?
92801.e: Depth and distance form a right-angled triangle. By Pythagoras, 30² + 40² = 900 + 1600 = 2500, and its square root is 50.
92801.m: You calculate the distance to the source with Pythagoras' theorem.

92802.q: What is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the hypocentre called?
92802.e: The hypocentre is inside the Earth. The point directly above it on the surface is called the epicentre, and the quake is often felt most strongly there.
92802.m: The epicentre is on the surface above the source of the quake.

92803.q: In which directions do earthquake waves spread from the hypocentre?
92803.e: From the source, the waves travel through the rock in all directions, like when you drop a stone into water. This is how they reach measuring stations all over the world.
92803.m: Earthquake waves spread from the source in all directions.

92804.q: Where do deep earthquakes mainly occur?
a: In subduction zones, where one plate sinks under another
92804.e: The sinking plate is colder and more brittle than the surrounding mantle. That is why ruptures can still happen in it at great depth.
92804.m: Deep earthquakes happen where tectonic plates sink down.

92805.q: Why does a shallow quake often cause more damage than an equally strong deep one?
a: The waves have a shorter path and lose less energy
Shallow quakes always last for days
Deep quakes never reach the surface
92805.e: Earthquake waves get weaker on their way through the rock. So with a nearby source, more energy arrives at the surface.
92805.m: Shallow earthquakes are often especially destructive at the surface.

92806.q: At what depth are the sources of most earthquakes in Switzerland?
92806.e: Swiss earthquakes happen in the Earth's crust. In the Alps, the sources are often even less than 15 km deep.
92806.m: Earthquakes in Switzerland mostly have shallow sources in the Earth's crust.

92807.q: What destroyed large parts of the city of Basel in 1356?
92807.e: On 18 October 1356, a strong earthquake shook the city of Basel. Afterwards, a big fire also broke out in the city.
92807.m: In 1356, an earthquake destroyed large parts of Basel.

92808.q: What destroyed a large part of the city's wooden houses after the Basel earthquake of 1356?
a: A fire in the city that lasted for days
92808.e: Overturned cooking fires and lamps set the city on fire. According to the sources, the fire raged for eight days.
92808.m: After the Basel earthquake, the city burned for days.

92809.q: Roughly where was the centre of the Basel earthquake of 1356?
92809.e: According to modern studies, the source of the quake was only a few kilometres south of Basel, near Reinach in Basel-Landschaft.
92809.m: The centre of the Basel earthquake was close to Basel.

92810.q: Which famous building in Basel was badly damaged in the earthquake of 1356?
92810.e: At Basel Minster, the choir collapsed and the roof fell into the nave. The other buildings did not even exist then.
92810.m: In 1356, Basel Minster was badly damaged.

92811.q: What happened to the castles in the wider area during the Basel earthquake?
a: Not a single one was hit
All stayed intact thanks to thick walls
They were all flooded by the Rhine
92811.e: Over a wide area around Basel, about 40 castles were badly hit. Many were rebuilt afterwards, others remained ruins.
92811.m: The Basel earthquake destroyed many castles in the region.

92812.q: Why did probably fewer people die in the Basel earthquake than you might expect?
a: Many had fled the city after a foreshock
The city was uninhabited at the time
All the houses were built to withstand earthquakes
It happened in the middle of the night
92812.e: A foreshock in the afternoon had warned people, and many left the city. Even so, the figures for the number of dead vary widely, between about 100 and 2000.
92812.m: A foreshock saved many people's lives in the Basel earthquake.

92813.q: What place does the Basel earthquake of 1356 hold in the history of Central Europe?
a: It is the strongest historically recorded quake
It is the most recent strong quake
It is the only quake with a tsunami
It is the weakest known quake
92813.e: No other recorded earthquake in Central Europe was as strong. That is why it serves as an important yardstick for the danger in the region.
92813.m: The Basel earthquake is the strongest recorded quake in Central Europe.

92814.q: Roughly what magnitude did the Basel earthquake of 1356 have, according to modern estimates?
92814.e: As there were no measuring instruments in 1356, the magnitude is estimated from the recorded damage. Estimates are between about 6 and 7; 6.6 is often given.
92814.m: According to estimates, the Basel earthquake had a magnitude between 6 and 7.

92815.q: How do we know so much today about the Basel earthquake of 1356, even though there were no measuring instruments?
a: From old reports and damage to buildings
From photos taken at the time
92815.e: Chroniclers wrote down what was destroyed, and on old walls such as at the Lohnhof you can still see damage from the quake today. Experts estimate the strength from this.
92815.m: Old reports and damage to buildings tell us about the Basel earthquake.

92816.q: What is the main task of the Swiss Seismological Service?
92816.e: The Seismological Service records all quakes in Switzerland and provides information about them. Its roots go back to the Earthquake Commission of 1878.
92816.m: The Swiss Seismological Service monitors earthquakes in Switzerland.

92817.q: Roughly how many seismic measuring stations does the Swiss Seismological Service run?
92817.e: The stations are spread across the whole country. Some are in caves, tunnels or boreholes.
92817.m: The Seismological Service monitors Switzerland with over 200 measuring stations.

92818.q: On average, how many earthquakes a year can people feel in Switzerland?
92818.e: Most recorded quakes are too weak to feel. Only 10 to 20 a year on average are noticed by the population.
92818.m: In Switzerland, about 10 to 20 earthquakes are felt each year.

92819.q: How quickly does the Swiss Seismological Service publish the first automatic information about a quake?
92819.e: The measurement data are analysed automatically. The location, time and strength appear on the website within about 90 seconds.
92819.m: The first information about a quake appears after about 90 seconds.

92820.q: Why can earthquake instruments also detect banned nuclear bomb tests?
a: Underground explosions shake the ground like earthquakes
Nuclear bombs send out radio waves
92820.e: Underground nuclear tests cause vibrations like earthquakes. A station near Davos is part of a worldwide network that monitors the ban on such tests.
92820.m: Seismometers also help to detect banned nuclear tests.

92821.q: In which app does the Swiss Seismological Service publish earthquake reports from magnitude 2.5?
92821.e: Quakes from magnitude 2.5 are also shown in the MeteoSwiss app. The service also provides information on its website and on naturgefahren.ch.
92821.m: Earthquake reports from magnitude 2.5 appear in the MeteoSwiss app.

92822.q: Who else does the Swiss Seismological Service inform about large damaging quakes abroad?
92822.e: After big disaster quakes anywhere in the world, help from Switzerland may be needed. That is why the Humanitarian Aid Unit is informed quickly.
92822.m: After big quakes abroad, the Seismological Service informs humanitarian aid.

92823.q: Who monitors earthquakes in Switzerland on behalf of the federal government?
a: The Seismological Service at ETH Zurich
The fire brigade of each municipality
92823.e: Since 1914, monitoring earthquakes has been a federal task. Today the Swiss Seismological Service is a unit of ETH Zurich.
92823.m: The Swiss Seismological Service is part of ETH Zurich.

92824.q: Roughly how often can an earthquake of magnitude 6 or more be expected in Switzerland?
92824.e: According to the Swiss Seismological Service, such strong quakes only happen every 50 to 150 years. But they could cause great damage.
92824.m: A magnitude 6 quake can be expected in Switzerland every 50 to 150 years.

92825.q: On average, how often can an earthquake that causes damage be expected in Switzerland?
92825.e: Damaging quakes are rarer in Switzerland than ones you can feel. According to the Swiss earthquake risk model, such a quake can be expected about every 8 to 15 years.
92825.m: A damaging quake happens in Switzerland about every 8 to 15 years.

92826.q: Besides Valais, which two regions are among those most at risk from earthquakes in Switzerland?
92826.e: Valais, the Grisons and the Basel region are most at risk. On the Swiss Plateau and in Ticino the risk is lower.
92826.m: Besides Valais, Basel and the Grisons are especially at risk from earthquakes.

92827.q: Which geological structure does Basel lie on, which explains the earthquake risk there?
92827.e: The Upper Rhine Graben is a zone where the Earth's crust is being pulled apart. The quakes there are only indirectly linked to the formation of the Alps.
92827.m: Basel lies on the earthquake-active Upper Rhine Graben.

92828.q: What do Swiss building standards require of new buildings today?
a: They must be built to withstand earthquakes
They may only be made of wood
They may have at most two storeys
They may not have a cellar
92828.e: Since 2003, modern rules for earthquake-resistant building have applied in Switzerland. New buildings must be designed so that they survive a quake well.
92828.m: New buildings in Switzerland must be built to withstand earthquakes.

92829.q: How much can soft ground such as lake deposits strengthen the shaking compared to rock?
a: Up to about a thousand times
92829.e: In soft ground, the waves build up. That is why areas on lake shores or in river valleys are more strongly affected in a quake.
92829.m: Soft ground can make shaking up to ten times stronger.

92830.q: Which way of building helps a building to survive an earthquake better?
a: A symmetrical floor plan and walls that run down to the foundations
As many large windows on the ground floor as possible
A heavy roof on thin supports
A different floor plan on every storey
92830.e: Load-bearing walls should run from the roof down to the foundations. A regular floor plan stops the building from twisting when it is shaken.
92830.m: Earthquake-proof houses have a regular floor plan and continuous walls.

92831.q: What does the Swiss earthquake risk model show?
a: What damage a quake could cause
Exactly when the next quake will come
Where there are volcanoes in Switzerland
What the weather will be like after a quake
92831.e: The risk model combines hazard, ground, building methods and population. It estimates what damage a quake could cause to people and buildings.
92831.m: The earthquake risk model estimates possible damage.

92832.q: Why is the earthquake risk higher in densely populated cities than in rural areas with the same hazard?
a: There are more people and buildings that can be harmed
The ground shakes more in cities
There are no earthquakes in the countryside
92832.e: The hazard only describes how often and how strongly the ground shakes. The risk also depends on how many people and assets would be affected.
92832.m: The more people and buildings are affected, the greater the earthquake risk.

92833.q: In which canton did the severe Visp earthquake of 1855 take place?
92833.e: The quake shook Upper Valais in 1855. It is probably the strongest earthquake in the history of Valais.
92833.m: The Visp earthquake of 1855 hit Valais.

92834.q: In which valley was the epicentre of the 1855 earthquake?
92834.e: The epicentre was in the Vispertal south of Visp. Many buildings there, including churches, were badly damaged.
92834.m: The epicentre of the 1855 quake was in the Vispertal.

92835.q: Roughly what magnitude did the Visp earthquake of 1855 have, according to modern estimates?
92835.e: Estimates are about 6.2 to 6.4. That makes it one of the strongest quakes in Switzerland in recent centuries.
92835.m: The Visp earthquake of 1855 had a magnitude of a little over 6.

92836.q: What did the 1855 earthquake trigger near St. Niklaus?
92836.e: The shaking loosened masses of rock near St. Niklaus. The only known victim of the quake was killed by falling rocks.
92836.m: The Visp quake triggered a rockfall near St. Niklaus.

92837.q: What followed the main Visp quake of 1855?
92837.e: After the main quake, the ground in the Vispertal shook many more times. This made the population even more anxious.
92837.m: The Visp earthquake was followed by many aftershocks.

92838.q: How far away could the Visp earthquake of 1855 be felt?
a: Throughout Switzerland and in neighbouring countries
Only in the village of Visp
Only in the canton of Valais
92838.e: The quake was felt throughout Switzerland. There are also reports from Savoy, northern Italy, the Tyrol and southern Germany.
92838.m: The Visp earthquake was felt far beyond Switzerland.

92839.q: What can an earthquake change about springs?
a: How much water flows out of them
The height of the mountains above them
92839.e: Earthquakes can change the paths of groundwater in the rock. After the Visp quake of 1855, some springs had a different amount of water.
92839.m: Earthquakes can make springs dry up or flow more strongly.

92840.q: What does the intensity of an earthquake describe?
a: How strong the effects are at a place
How deep the source of the earthquake is
92840.e: The intensity describes what people feel and what damage is done to buildings. In the Visp quake of 1855 there was severe damage to buildings.
92840.m: The intensity describes the effects of a quake at a place.

a: A mudflow of volcanic ash, rock and water
92841.e: A lahar forms when loose volcanic material mixes with water. It flows down the valleys like wet concrete.
92841.m: A lahar is a volcanic mudflow.

92842.q: Why is a lahar so destructive?
a: It is as heavy as wet concrete and sweeps houses away
It consists only of poisonous gas
It moves only a few metres per year
92842.e: A lahar is a thick mass of water, ash and rock. With great force it sweeps away bridges, houses and trees.
92842.m: Lahars are heavy and sweep everything away.

92843.q: Where do lahars usually flow down a volcano?
92843.e: Like water, lahars follow the land. They flow down stream beds and valleys, where there are often villages.

92844.q: Roughly how many people died from the lahars in Armero in 1985?
92844.e: Most of the inhabitants were taken by surprise in their sleep. It was one of the worst volcanic disasters of the 20th century.
92844.m: The lahar disaster of Armero claimed over 20,000 lives.

92845.q: What can cause a lahar even long after a volcanic eruption?
92845.e: Fresh ash lies loosely on the slopes. Heavy rain can turn it into a mudflow even years later.
92845.m: Heavy rain can trigger lahars even years after an eruption.

92846.q: Why are volcanoes covered by glaciers especially dangerous for lahars?
a: During an eruption, ice melts and provides lots of water
92846.e: Hot material melts snow and ice in a short time. The meltwater sweeps ash and rock along with it.
92846.m: Melting glaciers on volcanoes can feed huge lahars.

92847.q: What should you do if a lahar is coming?
a: Wait in the car in the valley
92847.e: Lahars flow in valleys and river beds. Anyone who quickly escapes to higher ground is safest.
92847.m: If a lahar comes, escape to higher ground.

92848.q: How can people in valleys below a volcano be warned about lahars in time?
92848.e: Measuring instruments in the valleys notice a mudflow early. Then sirens sound, and people have time to escape.
92848.m: Measuring instruments and sirens warn of lahars.

92849.q: How does a pyroclastic flow often form?
a: A column of ash or a lava dome collapses
Lava slowly cools in the sea
Rain washes ash into the valley
A glacier slides off the volcano
92849.e: If a column of ash becomes too heavy, it collapses. A breaking lava dome can also set off a glowing avalanche of gas, ash and rock.
92849.m: Pyroclastic flows often form when a column of ash or a lava dome collapses.

92850.q: How fast can a pyroclastic flow travel?
a: Over 100 km/h, sometimes several hundred km/h
About as fast as someone walking
92850.e: The hot mixture flows down the slope like a heavy gas. You cannot escape it on foot or by car.
92850.m: Pyroclastic flows are faster than any escape vehicle.

92851.q: How hot are pyroclastic flows typically?
92851.e: Temperatures are usually between about 200 and 700 degrees, sometimes even higher. That is enough to kill every living thing in their path.
92851.m: Pyroclastic flows are several hundred degrees hot.

92852.q: What destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre on the Caribbean island of Martinique in 1902?
a: A glowing cloud from the volcano Mont Pelée
92852.e: On 8 May 1902, a pyroclastic flow from Mont Pelée hit the town of Saint-Pierre. About 28,000 people died.
92852.m: In 1902, a glowing cloud from Mont Pelée destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre.

92853.q: Why is it deadly for volcanologists to film pyroclastic flows from close up?
a: The flows are extremely fast and hot
The flows are loud and damage hearing
92853.e: Pyroclastic flows race down the slope at over 100 km/h and several hundred degrees. In 1991, the scientists Katia and Maurice Krafft died this way on the Japanese volcano Unzen.

92854.q: What is another name for a pyroclastic flow?
92854.e: A pyroclastic flow is a red-hot cloud of gas, ash and rock. That is why it is also called a glowing cloud, in French “nuée ardente”.
92854.m: A pyroclastic flow is also called a glowing cloud.

92855.q: Which volcano destroyed the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum in the year 79?
92855.e: When Vesuvius erupted, pyroclastic flows hit the towns on the Bay of Naples. Hundreds of skeletons were later found on the beach at Herculaneum.
92855.m: Vesuvius destroyed Pompeii and Herculaneum in the year 79.

92856.q: Which volcano near Naples is monitored especially closely because so many people live near it?
92856.e: Millions of people live around Vesuvius. That is why it has had its own observatory watching it since 1841.
92856.m: Vesuvius is closely monitored because of the many people living nearby.

92857.q: What can it mean if the ground on a volcano slowly rises?
a: Magma is rising and collecting underground
The volcano is extinct for good
The volcano is sinking into the sea
92857.e: Rising magma pushes the rock above it upwards. With GPS devices and tilt meters, such uplift is measured to the millimetre.
92857.m: If the ground on a volcano rises, magma may be rising.

92858.q: Which gas do volcanologists measure especially often to detect changes in a volcano?
92858.e: When fresh magma rises, it gives off more sulphur dioxide. An increase can therefore signal an eruption.
92858.m: More sulphur dioxide can be a sign of rising magma.

92859.q: What do many small earthquakes under a volcano, so-called earthquake swarms, often indicate?
a: That the volcano is cooling down
That the volcano is growing without ever erupting
92859.e: When magma forces its way up, it breaks rock open. This causes many weak quakes, which seismometers on the volcano register.
92859.m: Earthquake swarms under a volcano can point to moving magma.

92860.q: What mainly decides how big a volcanic eruption is rated?
a: The amount of material thrown out
The time of day of the eruption
92860.e: Experts estimate how much ash and rock a volcano has thrown out. The more material, the higher the eruption is rated.
92860.m: The size of an eruption is measured by the amount of material thrown out.

92861.q: How do satellites measure ground changes on volcanoes from space?
92861.e: Radar satellites compare images of the same area taken at different times. This lets them detect uplift of a few centimetres over large areas.
92861.m: Radar satellites detect ground uplift on volcanoes from space.

92862.q: What do volcanologists use thermal imaging cameras for?
a: To spot hot places and fresh lava
To identify the colour of the ash
To count animals on the volcano
92862.e: Thermal cameras show differences in temperature even through smoke and at night. New hot spots can be a sign of an eruption.
92862.m: Thermal cameras show hot spots on volcanoes.

92863.q: In which group of islands is the very active volcano Kilauea?
92863.e: Kilauea is on the biggest island of Hawaii in the Pacific. It is one of the most active volcanoes in the world and has been monitored since 1912.
92863.m: Kilauea in Hawaii is one of the most active volcanoes.

92865.q: Which separation method is first used in a refinery to split crude oil into different fractions?
92865.e: The crude oil is heated strongly and evaporates. The parts condense at different heights in the column depending on their boiling point.
92865.m: Crude oil is separated into its fractions by fractional distillation.

92866.q: Where in the distillation column are the low-boiling fractions such as gases and petrol drawn off?
a: In the storage tank before it
92866.e: The column is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. Substances with a low boiling point rise highest before they condense.
92866.m: The lower the boiling point, the higher up a fraction is drawn off.

92867.q: Which thick residue is left at the bottom in oil distillation and is used for road surfaces?
92867.e: Bitumen has a very high boiling point and so does not evaporate. Mixed with stones and sand it makes asphalt.
92867.m: Bitumen is the heavy residue of crude oil and is found in asphalt.

92868.q: What is the process called in which long hydrocarbon molecules are split into shorter ones to get more petrol?
92868.e: Crude oil contains fewer short molecules than are needed for petrol. In cracking, long chains are broken into shorter ones using heat and catalysts.
92868.m: In cracking, long molecules are broken into shorter ones.

92869.q: From which crude oil fraction is the fuel for jet aircraft mainly obtained?
92869.e: Kerosene is a medium fraction that boils between petrol and diesel. It is used as aviation fuel for jet engines.

92870.q: Which two elements make up the hydrocarbons that form most of crude oil?
92870.e: The name gives it away: hydrocarbons are compounds of hydrogen and carbon. Crude oil is a mixture of a great many such compounds.
92870.m: Hydrocarbons consist of carbon and hydrogen.

92871.q: Why is sulfur removed from oil products in the refinery?
a: So that less sulfur dioxide forms when they burn
So that they flow faster through pipes
So that they get a lighter colour
So that they contain less energy
92871.e: Sulfur burns to form sulfur dioxide, which pollutes the air and contributes to acid rain. That is why it is removed beforehand.
92871.m: Fuels with the sulfur removed pollute the air less.

92872.q: What is the tall tower in a refinery in which crude oil is separated called?
92872.e: A distillation column has many trays stacked above one another. On each tray, a fraction with a similar boiling point collects.
92872.m: Crude oil is separated in a distillation column.

92873.q: For which type of engine is petrol the usual fuel?
92873.e: In a spark-ignition engine, a mixture of petrol and air is lit by a spark plug. Diesel engines, by contrast, ignite their fuel by compression.

92874.q: What does the octane rating of petrol tell you?
a: How much it costs per litre
92874.e: Knocking is uncontrolled self-ignition in the engine. The higher the octane rating, the better the petrol resists it.
92874.m: A high octane rating means petrol that resists knocking.

92875.q: What octane rating does the usual unleaded petrol at Swiss filling stations have?
92875.e: In Switzerland, standard petrol is called “Bleifrei 95” (unleaded 95). There is usually also a 98 octane type.
92875.m: Standard petrol in Switzerland has 95 octane.

92876.q: Why is lead no longer added to petrol today?
a: Lead is poisonous and ruins catalytic converters
92876.e: A lead compound used to make petrol resist knocking better. But lead is a poisonous heavy metal and makes catalytic converters useless.
92876.m: Petrol is unleaded today because lead is poisonous.

92877.q: Which two elements are the molecules in petrol mainly made of?
92877.e: Petrol is a mixture of hydrocarbons. These molecules are made of carbon and hydrogen atoms.

92878.q: Which substances mainly form when petrol burns completely?
92878.e: The carbon combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide, and the hydrogen forms water. A lot of energy is released.
92878.m: When petrol burns completely, carbon dioxide and water form.

92879.q: Roughly what is the density of petrol?
92879.e: Petrol is lighter than water, which weighs 1 kilogram per litre. That is why spilt petrol floats on water.

92880.q: Why is petrol very dangerous even at room temperature?
a: Its vapours form an explosive mixture with air
It freezes into ice at once
92880.e: Petrol evaporates easily. Even a small spark can set the vapours in the air alight.
92880.m: Petrol vapours can be lit by just a spark.

92881.q: From which raw material is petrol mainly obtained?
92881.e: Petrol is a fraction obtained from crude oil in the refinery. More petrol is also made by splitting longer molecules.
92881.m: Petrol is a crude oil product.

92882.q: What happens to a thermoplastic when you heat it?
a: It becomes soft and can be shaped
92882.e: Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be reshaped. When they cool, they become solid again.

92883.q: How are the molecules arranged in a thermoplastic?
a: As long chains that are not cross-linked
As ions in a crystal lattice
92883.e: The chains are only loosely connected to each other. When warm, they can slide past one another, which is why the material softens.
92883.m: Thermoplastics are made of chains that are not cross-linked.

92884.q: Which of these objects is usually made of a thermoplastic?
92884.e: PET is a plastic that softens when heated. So PET bottles can be melted down and made into new bottles.
92884.m: PET bottles are made of a plastic that can be melted.

92885.q: Why are thermoplastics easy to recycle?
a: They can be melted down and reshaped
They break down into crude oil by themselves
92885.e: Since thermoplastics melt when heated, they can be made into pellets. New products are then made from these.
92885.m: Thermoplastics can be melted down and reused.

92886.q: Which method is used to make many small thermoplastic parts in large numbers?
92886.e: In injection moulding, melted plastic is pressed into a mould under pressure. After cooling, the finished part drops out.
92886.m: Thermoplastics are often shaped by injection moulding.

92887.q: Which thermoplastic contains chlorine and is used for drainpipes and window frames?
92887.e: Polyvinyl chloride, PVC for short, has chlorine atoms in its chains. It is tough and weatherproof.
92887.m: PVC is a plastic that contains chlorine.

92888.q: Which thermoplastic is the white packaging foam made of that people in Switzerland often call “Sagex”?
92888.e: The foam is made of expanded polystyrene and contains a great deal of air. That is why it is light and insulates well.
92888.m: Packaging foam is usually made of expanded polystyrene.

92889.q: What is nylon, which ropes are made of, for example?
92889.e: Nylon was the first fully synthetic fibre and is a plastic. It is tear-resistant and elastic.

92890.q: What does the word part “thermo” in thermoplastic mean?
92890.e: “Thermos” is Greek and means warm. So a thermoplastic becomes plastic, that is mouldable, through heat.
92890.m: A thermoplastic can be shaped using heat.

92891.q: What happens to a thermoset when it is heated very strongly?
a: It becomes soft and can be shaped
It becomes as runny as water
92891.e: Thermosets cannot melt. If it gets too hot, the chemical bonds break and the material chars.
92891.m: Thermosets do not melt; they break down.

92892.q: How are the molecules in a thermoset connected to each other?
a: Loosely linked like a rubber band
Not at all, they are single atoms
92892.e: The chains are joined by many strong bonds into a dense network. That is why a thermoset is hard and keeps its shape.

92893.q: Which thermoset is considered the world’s first fully synthetic plastic?
92893.e: Bakelite was invented at the start of the 20th century. It was used, for example, for old telephones and radio cases.
92893.m: Bakelite was the first fully synthetic plastic.

92894.q: What was the plastic Bakelite used for in the past, for example?
92894.e: Bakelite is hard, heat-resistant and insulates against electricity. So it was used for the cases of telephones, radios and plugs.
92894.m: Many telephones used to be made of Bakelite.

92895.q: Why are pan handles and sockets often made of thermoset plastic?
a: Because it resists heat and does not melt
92895.e: Thermosets keep their shape even when warm. They also insulate electrically, which makes them suitable for sockets.
92895.m: Thermosets are suitable for hot handles and electrical parts.

92896.q: Which material, with synthetic resin as its binder, is used for boat hulls and wind turbine blades?
92896.e: In glass-fibre reinforced plastic, hardened resins hold the glass fibres together. The material is light and very strong.
92896.m: Glass-fibre reinforced plastic is light and strong.

92897.q: Which glue hardens into a thermoset after two components are mixed?
92897.e: In epoxy resin glue, the resin and hardener react with each other. A firmly cross-linked plastic forms that no longer melts.
92897.m: Epoxy resin glue hardens into a thermoset.

92898.q: Which group of plastics is only loosely cross-linked and therefore stretchy like rubber?
92898.e: Elastomers such as rubber can be stretched and spring back. Their chains are linked at only a few points.
92898.m: Elastomers are loosely cross-linked and stretchy.

92899.q: Which small molecule is polyethylene made from?
92899.e: Ethene, also called ethylene, has a double bond. Many ethene molecules join together to form long chains.
92899.m: Polyethylene is made from many ethene molecules.

92900.q: What is the reaction called in which many small molecules join to form a long chain?
92900.e: In polymerisation, monomers are linked to form a polymer. “Poly” means many.
92900.m: In polymerisation, small molecules form long chains.

92901.q: Which plastic is produced in the largest amount worldwide?
92901.e: Polyethylene is cheap, light and versatile. It is found in films, bags, bottles and pipes.
92901.m: Polyethylene is the most produced plastic in the world.

92902.q: Why is polyethylene good for shampoo and detergent bottles?
a: It falls apart in a few days
92902.e: Polyethylene is tough, does not break and lets no water through. So many bottles for the bathroom and household are made of it.

92903.q: Which kind of polyethylene are soft films and plastic bags usually made of?
92903.e: In low-density polyethylene (LDPE) the chains are highly branched. So they lie more loosely and the material is soft.
92903.m: Soft films are usually made of LDPE.

92904.q: Which elements is polyethylene made of?
92904.e: The chain of polyethylene consists of carbon atoms with hydrogen atoms attached. No other elements are present.

92905.q: Why does a piece of polyethylene float on water?
a: Its density is lower than that of water
92905.e: Polyethylene has a density of about 0.91 to 0.97 grams per cubic centimetre. Water has 1 gram per cubic centimetre.
92905.m: Polyethylene floats because it is less dense than water.

92906.q: What is polyethylene often used for in everyday life?
92906.e: Polyethylene is cheap, light and flexible. It is used to make bags, films, bottles and pipes.
92906.m: Plastic bags and films are often made of polyethylene.

92907.q: How is a PET bottle formed from a small, thick-walled blank?
a: By stretch blow moulding with compressed air
By casting in a sand mould
92907.e: The blank is warmed, placed in a mould and blown up with compressed air. The material is stretched and the bottle gets its shape.
92907.m: PET bottles are blown up from warmed blanks.

92908.q: Why should you squash PET bottles flat before collecting them?
a: So they take up less space during transport
So they become lighter in colour
92908.e: Squashed bottles take up much less volume. So more bottles fit into collection bags and lorries.
92908.m: Flattened PET bottles save space during transport.

92909.q: Roughly what was the recycling rate for PET drinks bottles in Switzerland in 2024?
92909.e: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, over 84 per cent of PET drinks bottles were recycled in 2024. The law requires at least 75 per cent.
92909.m: In Switzerland, over 80 per cent of PET bottles are recycled.

92910.q: Under which name is PET used as a textile fibre for fleece jackets?
92910.e: PET is one of the polyesters. As a fibre it is tear-resistant, light and dries quickly.

92911.q: From which raw material is PET mainly made?
92911.e: The starting materials for PET come from the petrochemical industry. Today, a small part can also come from plants.
92911.m: PET is mostly made from crude oil.

92912.q: Which properties make PET especially suitable for drinks bottles?
92912.e: PET bottles weigh much less than glass bottles and do not break. They are also clear and hold in the fizz well.
92912.m: PET is light, unbreakable and clear.

92913.q: Which group of plastics does PET belong to?
92913.e: PET softens when heated and can be reshaped. When it cools, it becomes solid again.

92914.q: Where do you take empty PET drinks bottles in Switzerland?
92914.e: Almost every shop that sells drinks in PET has a collection point. The collected bottles are made into new bottles or fibres.
92914.m: PET bottles belong in the PET collection.

92915.q: Which number in the recycling triangle stands for PET?
92915.e: Plastics are marked with numbers in the recycling triangle. PET has the number 1.
92915.m: PET has the number 1 in the recycling triangle.

92917.q: By which everyday name is glucose known?
92917.e: Glucose is found in large amounts in grapes. That is where the name grape sugar comes from.
92917.m: Glucose is also known as grape sugar.

92918.q: How sweet does glucose taste compared with ordinary table sugar?
92918.e: Glucose has only about two thirds to three quarters of the sweetness of table sugar. Fructose, on the other hand, tastes sweeter than table sugar.
92918.m: Glucose is a little less sweet than table sugar.

92920.q: Which group of nutrients does glucose belong to?
92920.e: Glucose is a simple sugar and therefore the simplest carbohydrate. It is the most important energy supplier for cells.

92921.q: What forms when yeast ferments glucose without oxygen?
92921.e: In alcoholic fermentation, yeast turns sugar into alcohol and gas. The gas also makes bread dough rise.
92921.m: Yeast ferments sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide.

92922.q: Which hormone lowers the amount of glucose in the blood?
92922.e: Insulin is made in the pancreas. It makes the cells take up glucose from the blood.

92924.q: What colour does iodine solution turn when you drip it onto starch?
92924.e: Iodine fits inside the spiral-shaped starch molecules. This produces a deep blue to black colour.

92925.q: What building blocks is starch made of?
92925.e: Starch consists of hundreds to thousands of linked glucose units. During digestion it is broken back down into these building blocks.
92925.m: Starch is built from glucose units.

92926.q: In which part of the potato plant is starch stored as a reserve?
92926.e: The potato tuber grows underground and is a storage organ. It contains a lot of starch as an energy store for new shoots.

92927.q: What is starch in our food mainly for?
92927.e: During digestion, starch is broken down into glucose. The body uses this sugar as energy for the muscles and brain.

92928.q: What happens when you heat starch in water, for example to thicken a sauce?
a: It swells and thickens the liquid
92928.e: When heated, the starch grains take up water and burst. The starch turns gel-like and the liquid becomes thick.
92928.m: Heated starch binds water and thickens sauces.

92929.q: Which of these foods contains a lot of starch?
92929.e: Rice, pasta, bread and potatoes are rich in starch. Cucumbers are mostly water, butter is mostly fat.
92929.m: Rice, bread and pasta contain a lot of starch.

92930.q: Which substance is built from glucose like starch, but cannot be digested by humans?
92930.e: Cellulose forms the cell walls of plants and is found in wood and paper. Our body cannot split its bonds; it serves as dietary fibre.
92930.m: For humans, cellulose is indigestible fibre.

92931.q: Which type of carbohydrate is starch?
92931.e: Starch consists of a great many linked sugar units. Such carbohydrates are called polysaccharides.

92933.q: Which simple test can show fat in foods?
92933.e: If you rub the food on paper, fat leaves a see-through spot. A water spot disappears again as it dries.
92933.m: Fat leaves a see-through spot on paper.

92934.q: What makes oils different from solid fats such as butter?
a: Oils are liquid at room temperature
Oils are made of amino acids
92934.e: Chemically, oils and fats are built the same way. Oils contain more unsaturated fatty acids and therefore have a lower melting point.

92935.q: What is the reaction of fat with sodium hydroxide solution, which produces soap, called?
92935.e: The alkali splits the fat into glycerol and salts of fatty acids. These salts are the soap.
92935.m: In saponification, fat and alkali make soap.

92936.q: Apart from storing energy, what job does fatty tissue do in the body?
a: It protects organs and insulates against cold
It carries oxygen in the blood
It carries nerve signals to the brain
92936.e: Fat pads surround the kidneys, for example, and cushion knocks. Under the skin, a layer of fat keeps body heat in.
92936.m: Fatty tissue protects organs and keeps you warm.

92937.q: Roughly how much energy does 1 gram of fat provide?
92937.e: Fat provides around 9 kilocalories or 37 kilojoules per gram. That is about twice as much as carbohydrates or proteins.
92937.m: Fat is the most energy-rich nutrient.

92938.q: Why do butter and cooking oil go rancid over time?
a: Fats are broken down by oxygen, light and heat
Fats take up salt from the air
92938.e: Unsaturated fatty acids in particular react with oxygen. This produces substances that smell and taste unpleasant.
92938.m: Store fats cool, dark and sealed so they do not go rancid.

92939.q: Which fatty acids contain double bonds and are found especially in plant oils?
92939.e: Double bonds put kinks in the fatty acid chains. So the molecules pack together less tightly.
92939.m: Unsaturated fatty acids have double bonds.

92940.q: What building blocks are proteins made of?
92940.e: Proteins are long chains of amino acids. The order of the amino acids decides the shape and job of the protein.
92940.m: Proteins are built from amino acids.

92941.q: Roughly how many different amino acids does the human body use to build proteins?
92941.e: Humans build their proteins from around 20 different amino acids. Some of these must be taken in with food.
92941.m: Proteins are built from around 20 amino acids.

92942.q: Why does runny egg white turn solid and white when you cook an egg?
a: The proteins are denatured by the heat
92942.e: Heat destroys the three-dimensional shape of the proteins. The chains clump together and the egg white becomes solid and opaque.

92943.q: Which element is found in all proteins but not in fats and sugars?
92943.e: Every amino acid has an amino group containing nitrogen. Fats and carbohydrates consist only of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

92944.q: Which of these foods contains the most protein?
92944.e: Dairy products such as quark, as well as meat, eggs and pulses, contain a lot of protein. Fruit, vegetables and sugar provide hardly any protein.

92945.q: What does our body mainly need proteins for?
92945.e: Proteins are the body’s most important building materials. Muscles, skin and many parts of cells are made of them.
92945.m: Proteins are building materials for muscles and cells.

92946.q: Which protein makes up hair and fingernails?
92946.e: Keratin is a tough fibrous protein. It is also found in feathers, hooves and horns.
92946.m: Hair and nails are made of keratin.

92947.q: Which milk protein curdles when rennet is added in cheese-making?
92947.e: Rennet makes the casein in milk clump together. It forms the solid cheese curd; the liquid separated off is the whey.
92947.m: Cheese is made from the milk protein casein.

92948.q: How is a surfactant molecule built?
a: A water-loving head and a fat-loving tail
A metal core with a shell
92948.e: The head is hydrophilic and is drawn into the water. The long tail is hydrophobic and attaches to fat.
92948.m: Surfactants have a water-loving part and a fat-loving part.

92949.q: What do surfactants do at the surface of water?
92949.e: Surfactants gather at the surface and weaken the hold between water molecules. This lets water wet things better.
92949.m: Surfactants reduce the surface tension of water.

92950.q: What do surfactants do with droplets of fat when washing up?
a: They surround the fat so it is rinsed away
They make the fat go hard
They turn the fat into water
They stick the fat to the plate
92950.e: The fat-loving ends of the surfactants attach to the fat, and the water-loving ends point outwards. So the fat floats in the water and is rinsed away.
92950.m: Surfactants surround fat so water can rinse it away.

92951.q: In which products are surfactants the most important active ingredient?
92951.e: Surfactants loosen fat and dirt from surfaces and fabrics. That is why they are the main ingredient of cleaning products.
92951.m: Detergents and washing-up liquids clean with surfactants.

92952.q: What is the oldest surfactant made by humans?
92952.e: Soap has been made for thousands of years. Modern synthetic surfactants have only existed since the 20th century.

92953.q: How does a solution of classic hard soap in water react?
92953.e: Soaps are salts of weak fatty acids. In water they form a slightly alkaline solution with a pH above 7.

92954.q: Which property must surfactants in detergents have today so that they do not harm rivers and lakes?
a: They must be insoluble in water
92954.e: In the past, surfactants that broke down poorly formed mountains of foam on rivers. Today, surfactants must break down in sewage works and in water.

92955.q: What do you call a finely spread mixture of oil in water, which surfactants can stabilise?
92955.e: In an emulsion, small droplets of one liquid are spread through another. Milk and mayonnaise are examples.
92955.m: An emulsion is a mixture of two liquids that do not mix.

92956.q: Which substance is the main ingredient of methylated spirits?
92956.e: Methylated spirits consist mostly of ethanol, the same alcohol as in alcoholic drinks. But it has been made undrinkable.
92956.m: Methylated spirits consist mainly of ethanol.

a: So that nobody uses it as drinking alcohol
So that it burns more brightly
So that it evaporates less quickly
92957.e: Denatured alcohol tastes and smells so bad that it cannot be drunk. In return, it is not taxed like drinking alcohol.
92957.m: Denatured alcohol has been made undrinkable.

92958.q: What does denatured methylated spirits taste like?
92958.e: When denaturing, bitter substances are added. Even tiny amounts make the spirits undrinkable.
92958.m: Bitter substances make methylated spirits undrinkable.

92959.q: Why does methylated spirits feel cold on your skin?
a: It evaporates quickly and takes heat from the skin
It is kept in the fridge
It conducts electricity away from the skin
92959.e: A liquid needs energy to evaporate. The spirits take this heat from the skin, which cools down as a result.

92960.q: What is the formula of ethanol?
92960.e: An ethanol molecule contains two carbon atoms, six hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. The formula is written so that you can see the structure.

92961.q: What is methylated spirits often used for in Swiss households?
a: As fuel for the fondue burner
As heating oil for central heating
92961.e: In the fondue burner, methylated spirits burns and keeps the fondue warm. It is also used to clean glass.
92961.m: Methylated spirits heats the fondue burner.

92962.q: Why is the flame of burning spirits especially treacherous?
a: It is almost invisible in daylight
92962.e: Ethanol burns with a faint blue flame that hardly makes soot. It is easy to miss that something is still burning.
92962.m: Flames from spirits are hard to see in daylight.

92963.q: Why must you never pour methylated spirits into a fondue burner that is still burning or hot?
a: The vapours catch fire and there is a sudden flash of flame
92963.e: The spirits evaporate at once on the hot spot. The flame can flash back through the vapours into the bottle and cause serious burns.
92963.m: Only refill a fondue burner when it is cold and out.

93163.e: There are many varieties of apple. Their skin can be red, yellow, green or a mix.
93163.m: Apples can be red, yellow or green.

93164.q: Which canton has lots of apple trees and is therefore jokingly called “Mostindien”?
93164.e: There are especially many apple trees in Thurgau. Because a lot of apple juice and cider (Most) is made there, it is jokingly called “Mostindien”.

93165.q: What is the soft purée made from cooked apples called?
93165.e: You cook pieces of apple until soft and mash them. This makes apple sauce.
93165.m: Apple sauce is made from cooked apples.

93166.q: Why does a cut apple turn brown after a while?
a: Because air gets to the flesh
93166.e: Substances in the flesh react with the air. This creates the brown colour.

93167.q: What can you drizzle on apple slices so they do not turn brown so quickly?
93167.e: Lemon juice slows down the browning. This keeps the slices pale for longer.
93167.m: Lemon juice keeps apple slices pale.

93168.q: What happens to an apple if you put it in a bucket of water?
93168.e: An apple contains a lot of air between its cells. That is why it is lighter than water and floats.

93169.q: Who usually lives in an apple with a “worm” in it?
93169.e: The “worm” in the apple is actually the caterpillar of a small moth. It eats its way through the flesh.
93169.m: The worm in the apple is actually a caterpillar.

93170.q: In the legend, which fruit did William Tell shoot from his son's head?
93170.e: In the legend, Tell had to shoot an apple from the head of his son Walter with his crossbow. He hit it.
93170.m: William Tell shot an apple from his son's head.

93171.q: Which insects mainly pollinate the flowers of apple trees?
93171.e: Bees fly from flower to flower and carry the pollen with them. This is the only way lots of apples can grow.

93172.q: What shape is a typical pear?
a: Fat at the bottom, narrow at the top
93172.e: A pear is rounded at the bottom and gets narrower towards the stalk at the top. That makes it easy to recognise.
93172.m: A pear is fat at the bottom and narrow at the top.

93173.q: Which canton is known for its Williams pears?
93173.e: Lots of Williams pears grow in sunny Valais. They are very juicy and smell strongly.
93173.m: Valais is known for Williams pears.

93175.q: Which fruit is the pear closely related to?
93175.e: Pears and apples belong to the same plant family, the rose family. Both grow on trees here.
93175.m: Pears and apples are close relatives.

93176.q: Which group of fruit does the pear belong to, because it has a core inside?
93176.e: Fruits with a core and small pips are called pome fruits. The quince, for example, is one too.
93176.m: The pear is a pome fruit.

93177.q: What happens to a hard pear if it lies in the kitchen for a few days?
93177.e: Pears keep ripening after they are picked. That is why they get soft and sweet in the kitchen.

93178.q: Why do some pears feel a bit gritty when you eat them?
a: Because of sand in the skin
Because of sugar on the skin
93178.e: In the flesh of the pear there are tiny hard cells. They are called stone cells, and you can feel them when you chew.
93178.m: Small stone cells make pears a bit gritty.

93179.q: What is a Swiss bake with a filling of dried pears called?
